title: Example: Pride and Prejudice (ch. I–VIII)
notes:
# Sample notes (written for this example, not a real reader's)

## Chapter I

> It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune must be in want of a wife. [p. 2]

The opening line is ironic: it's really the neighbourhood families who are in want of the single man's fortune, not the other way round.

Mr. Bennet answers every one of his wife's worries with a joke instead of an answer. Funny, but is he ever actually going to do anything for his daughters?

## Chapter III

Bingley dances every dance and Darcy refuses almost everyone [p. 9]. The book is setting them up as opposites: warm versus cold.

Elizabeth laughs it off and tells the story to her friends. It clearly doesn't bother her.

## Chapter VI

Charlotte says Jane should show more affection than she feels. That's cynical, but maybe also realistic about how little time women here get to secure a match.

## Chapter VII

entail — an estate settled on male heirs only

So the Bennet girls' panic about marriage is completely rational, and Mrs. Bennet is the only one in the house facing it.

## Chapter VIII

Elizabeth walking three miles through the mud to Netherfield shows she doesn't care what anyone thinks of her.

cards.text: I show you his answer in the very next chapter: he visits Bingley in secret, then teases his wife about it [p. 6]. Is a joke the only way he can do something?
cards.anchor: is he ever actually going to do anything for his daughters?

cards.text: Is Darcy cold, or only unable to perform? He says he detests dancing without a familiar partner [p. 12]. Bingley's warmth also spreads evenly to everyone. Is that warmth, or ease?
Is she facing it, or only chasing it? Her plan rests on Bingley's "four or five thousand a year" [p. 3], not on any thrift. Mr. Bennet's jokes might be his way of facing it too.
